Thus I = ∫_0^{2π} (q t sin t) / (p + q cos t) dt.

This looks like an integrand that can be expressed as derivative with respect to something of a log, since derivative of ln(p+q cos t) = -(q sin t)/(p+q cos t). Indeed, d/dt ln(p+q cos t) = -(q sin t)/(p+q cos t). Because derivative cos t = -sin t; so derivative of p+q cos t = -q sin t, dividing yields -(q sin t)/(p+q cos t). So (q sin t)/(p+q cos t) = - d/dt [ln(p+q cos t)]. So integrand is - t * d/dt [ln(p+q cos t)].

Thus I = ∫_0^{2π} -t * d/dt ln(p+q cos t) dt = - ∫_0^{2π} t d/dt[ln(p+q cos t)] dt. This suggests integration by parts: let u = t, dv = d[ln(p+q cos t)]*? Actually dv = d/dt[ln(p+q cos t)] dt. Then we can do integral ∫ t f'(t) dt = t f(t) - ∫ f(t) dt.

Thus I = - [t * ln(p+q cos t)]_0^{2π} + ∫_0^{2π} ln(p+q cos t) dt. So I = -[t ln(p+q cos t)]_0^{2π} + ∫_0^{2π} ln(p+q cos t) dt.

Now evaluate the boundary term: At t = 0: cos 0 = 1, so p+q cos 0 = p+q. At t = 2π: cos 2π = 1, so p+q cos 2π = p+q also. So ln(p+q) same at both ends. So term: at upper limit 2π * ln(p+q) minus at lower limit 0 * ln(p+q) = 2π ln(p+q) - 0 = 2π ln(p+q). So negative of that: I = -[2π ln(p+q) - 0] + ∫_0^{2π} ln(p+q cos t) dt = -2π ln(p+q) + ∫_0^{2π} ln(p+q cos t) dt.

Thus I = ∫_0^{2π} ln(p+q cos t) dt - 2π ln(p+q). However, note that the answer is likely expressed in terms of known integrals of log. There is standard integral: ∫_0^{2π} ln(p + q cos t) dt = 2π ln[(p + sqrt(p^2 - q^2))/2]? Actually known formula: For p > |q| > 0, ∫_0^{2π} log(p + q cos θ) dθ = 2π ln( (p + √(p^2 - q^2)) / 2 ). Let’s verify: The standard result is ∫_0^{2π} log (a + b cos θ) dθ = 2π log [ (a + √(a^2 - b^2))/2 ] for a > |b|. Yes this is known. So we can apply with a = p, b = q.

Thus ∫_0^{2π} ln(p + q cos t) dt = 2π ln( (p + √(p^2 - q^2))/2 ).

Thus I = 2π ln( (p + √(p^2 - q^2))/2 ) - 2π ln(p+q) = 2π [ ln( (p + √(p^2 - q^2))/2 ) - ln(p+q) ] = 2π ln( (p + √(p^2 - q^2))/ [2(p+q)] ).

Simplify: I = 2π ln( (p + √(p^2 - q^2)) / (2(p+q)) ). That is the final answer.

I=\int_{0}^{2\pi}\frac{q\,t\sin t}{p+q\cos t}\,dt ,\qquad p>q>0
\]

---

**Step 1 – Write the integrand as a derivative.**  

\[
\frac{q\sin t}{p+q\cos t}= -\frac{d}{dt}\ln\!\bigl(p+q\cos t\bigr) .
\]

Hence  

\[
I=-\int_{0}^{2\pi} t\,\frac{d}{dt}\ln\!\bigl(p+q\cos t\bigr)\,dt .
\]

---

**Step 2 – Integration by parts.**  

Let  

\[
u=t,\qquad dv=\frac{d}{dt}\ln\!\bigl(p+q\cos t\bigr)\,dt .
\]

Then \(du=dt\) and \(v=\ln\!\bigl(p+q\cos t\bigr)\).  
Thus  

\[
\begin{aligned}
I &=-\Bigl[t\ln\!\bigl(p+q\cos t\bigr)\Bigr]_{0}^{2\pi}
   +\int_{0}^{2\pi}\ln\!\bigl(p+q\cos t\bigr)\,dt .
\end{aligned}
\]

Because \(\cos0=\cos2\pi=1\),

\[
\Bigl[t\ln\!\bigl(p+q\cos t\bigr)\Bigr]_{0}^{2\pi}
  =2\pi\ln(p+q)-0 .
\]

Hence  

\[
I =\int_{0}^{2\pi}\ln\!\bigl(p+q\cos t\bigr)\,dt -2\pi\ln(p+q).
\]

---

**Step 3 – Use the known logarithmic integral.**  

For \(a>|b|\) (here \(a=p,\;b=q\)) the classic result (Poisson’s integral) is  

\[
\int_{0}^{2\pi}\ln\!\bigl(a+b\cos t\bigr)\,dt
     =2\pi\ln\!\frac{a+\sqrt{a^{2}-b^{2}}}{2}.
\]

Applying it:

\[
\int_{0}^{2\pi}\ln\!\bigl(p+q\cos t\bigr)\,dt
     =2\pi\ln\!\frac{p+\sqrt{p^{2}-q^{2}}}{2}.
\]

---

**Step 4 – Assemble the result.**  

\[
\begin{aligned}
I &=2\pi\ln\!\frac{p+\sqrt{p^{2}-q^{2}}}{2}
      -2\pi\ln(p+q)\\[4pt]
  &=2\pi\ln\!\left(\frac{p+\sqrt{p^{2}-q^{2}}}{2(p+q)}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(p>q>0\), the argument of the logarithm is \<1, so the integral is negative, as expected.

\[
\boxed{\,\displaystyle I
=2\pi\ln\!\left(\frac{p+\sqrt{p^{2}-q^{2}}}{2\,(p+q)}\right)\,}
\]<|eot_id|> <|end_of_text|>
